Finding: At least 79 original activity images across six albums include identifiable people; visual review confirmed recognizable elementary-age students in five in-person school albums and identifiable adults in the online album. No consent ledger is present in the repository.
Impact: Public Git history would permanently associate identifiable children with schools and classroom activities; publication may violate consent or safeguarding expectations.
Remediation: Obtain and record explicit publication authorization per image/person or remove/anonymize the affected media; review both current content and history.

File: public/resources/METC/活动成果展览/{上步小学,梅丽小学}/**
Finding: Seventeen current images contain GPSLatitude and GPSLongitude EXIF fields; dates, device details, and host-computer metadata also occur.
Impact: A public clone permits extraction of precise capture locations linked to children, schools, and dates.
Remediation: Strip sensitive EXIF from approved derivatives, replace the committed blobs, and remove the original metadata-bearing blobs from reachable history.

Finding: Three named student leaders are published with unique school email addresses whose local parts contain student-number identifiers; the values are embedded in browser output.
Impact: Public source and bundles facilitate harvesting, profiling, phishing, and student-ID correlation.
Remediation: Use role-based aliases or obtain documented consent; remove/redact current and historical personal addresses if not expressly approved.

Finding: The R2 migration deletion in 522861a did not survive integration: origin/main still contains 411 public-resource files, about 483 MiB of regular Git blobs plus 472 MiB of LFS payloads, including originals, Office sources, PDFs, HEIC, photos, and video.
Impact: Making the repository public exposes the complete raw corpus; enabling GitHub Pages would also copy regular public/ resources into the site artifact, contrary to documentation that says resources are R2-only.
Remediation: Define a public-content allowlist, move private/raw sources outside the public repository and public/ tree, repair generation paths, and clean reachable Git/LFS history.

Finding: GitHub records 28 Vercel-style bot deployments across multiple Preview and Production environment variants; those environments have no protection rules. Fork-PR deployment approval and Vercel environment-variable scoping could not be verified.
Impact: After publication, an external PR could become a secret-exfiltration or malicious-preview path if any linked Vercel project builds fork code with privileged variables.
Remediation: Inventory and remove duplicate Vercel projects, disable or require approval for fork previews, scope Preview variables to non-privileged values, protect Production, and test with a benign fork before release.

Finding: Thirteen of 17 current OOXML source files contain non-generic creator or last-modified identities; eight generated/source PDFs contain Author fields and all 16 unique PDFs contain other metadata. No comments, tracked changes, macros, embedded objects, form fields, or executable PDF JavaScript were confirmed.
Impact: Personal author identities and workstation history become searchable and permanently attributable in public Git/LFS history.
Remediation: Review and scrub approved Office/PDF metadata, regenerate previews from scrubbed sources, and clean old Git/LFS objects if identities are not approved for publication.

Finding: Of 123 reachable commits, 120 use non-noreply author addresses: consumer-mail domains or a local workstation hostname across three identities.
Impact: Public Git history exposes personal addresses and a machine-name identifier to scraping and phishing.
Remediation: Obtain author consent or rewrite author metadata to approved noreply/organizational identities before publication; configure future contributors to use noreply addresses.

Finding: The browser fetches HTML from the public R2 host and injects it with dangerouslySetInnerHTML. The generation sanitizer is allowlist-based, but there is no runtime sanitizer or CSP and an out-of-band R2 replacement bypasses generation.
Impact: Compromise or misconfiguration of R2 write access could turn a syllabus object into stored DOM XSS on the site origin.
Remediation: Verify anonymous writes are impossible; integrity-control the publishing pipeline; sanitize fetched markup at runtime or render structured data; deploy a restrictive CSP where supported.

Finding: The build job inherits pages:write and id-token:write, installs with npm without the tracked pnpm lockfile, uses semver ranges, and references action major tags rather than commit SHAs. Repository Actions permit all actions and do not require SHA pinning.
Impact: A registry/action compromise or trusted-main compromise receives unnecessary deployment/OIDC capability and produces a non-reproducible build.
Remediation: Give build contents:read only; grant Pages/OIDC only to deploy; restore pnpm frozen-lockfile; pin actions to reviewed SHAs; restrict allowed actions.

Finding: pnpm audit reported 0 critical, 9 high, and 7 moderate advisories in next 16.2.10 and transitive sharp, postcss, and nanoid. The audited static app has no Server Actions, middleware, dynamic image optimization, or untrusted CSS processing, so the high advisory paths were not practically reachable in the deployed architecture.
Impact: Known vulnerable versions increase future risk and build-time exposure if the architecture or content pipeline changes.
Remediation: Update to patched Next.js and transitive versions, regenerate the lockfile, rerun build/typecheck/audit, and keep automated dependency alerts enabled.

Finding: Ignore rules omit .env*, .vercel/, private-key and credential-file patterns. Historical commits contain tsconfig.tsbuildinfo, Playwright state snapshots, and many generated screenshots.
Impact: A public contribution workflow has elevated risk of accidental credential, local deployment metadata, or generated-state commits.
Remediation: Add scoped ignore rules while retaining an explicit .env.example exception; add pre-commit/CI secret scanning; review generated artifacts before history cleanup.

Finding: Secret scanning is disabled; code scanning/Advanced Security is not enabled; no SECURITY.md or CODEOWNERS exists; branch protection/rulesets are unavailable on the current private-plan state; allowed Actions are unrestricted and SHA pinning is not required.
Impact: A newly public repository would lack core prevention, review, ownership, and disclosure controls during its highest-risk transition period.
Remediation: After privacy/history remediation, enable public-repo security features and an enforceable main ruleset, restrict Actions, add SECURITY.md/CODEOWNERS, and verify settings before accepting contributions.

Finding: Maintainers are instructed to process contributed DOCX/PPTX/PDF/HEIC files with LibreOffice, Poppler, Pillow, and sips on local machines without sandboxing or malware screening.
Impact: A malicious public contributor could submit a parser exploit or decompression bomb and persuade a maintainer to run the pipeline.
Remediation: Treat contributed binaries as hostile; require review, size/type limits and malware scanning; process in a disposable least-privileged container/VM with patched converters.

Finding: No repository-controlled CSP, frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, or nosniff policy is defined. GitHub Pages and Vercel header behavior differs and static export limits Next.js header configuration.
Impact: Missing defense-in-depth increases the impact of content injection and permits framing where the host does not add protection.
Remediation: Choose the production host, configure supported response headers at that host, or add an appropriate meta CSP for directives it can enforce; verify live responses.

Finding: Documentation contradicts the current tree and live deployment state, claims resources are absent/R2-only, and includes a personal local filesystem username and internal workstation paths.
Impact: Operators may unintentionally publish raw content or follow unsafe assumptions; personal developer metadata becomes public.
Remediation: Reconcile docs with the chosen deployment/resource model and replace personal absolute paths with neutral placeholders.

Finding: GitHub Pages is currently disabled while the workflow still deploys to Pages; the three latest runs built successfully but deployment failed with HTTP 404.
Impact: Security controls and public-resource behavior cannot be validated against a stable live GitHub Pages deployment, and operators may mistake a successful build for release.
Remediation: Select one supported production path, enable and protect it intentionally, retire stale deployment integrations, and perform post-deploy header/content verification.
